claims.text: High-energy planetary ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering can process an NbMoCrTiAl RHEA composite.
The combined ball-milling and SPS process enables large-scale reactive processing.
The combined process produces a stable microstructure despite the positive heat of mixing between Cu and refractory elements.
The starting material is powdered NbMoCrTiAl RHEA.
Cu can be included in the powdered NbMoCrTiAl starting material for this process.
A process control agent such as stearic acid is used during high-energy planetary ball milling.
Ball milling is performed at approximately 300 rpm for 39 hours.
SPS consolidation is performed at approximately 1700 °C under 30 MPa for 30 minutes.
The milling and SPS operations are conducted in an inert or vacuum environment.
TiC and Al2O3 reinforcing phases form in situ in the NbMoCrTiAl matrix.
The TiC and Al2O3 phases limit excessive diffusion and segregation.
High-energy milling refines the powder.
High-energy milling uniformly distributes elements that would otherwise segregate.
Rapid SPS limits diffusion-driven segregation.
The ceramic reinforcements pin grain boundaries and act as barriers to phase separation.
The processed NbMoCrTiAl composite has approximately 50% greater compressive fracture strength than its as-cast counterpart.
The process produces a controlled distribution of phases including Cu inclusions.
As-cast RHEAs containing both refractory elements and Cu are prone to segregation because of positive heat of mixing.
Excessively high Cu content can cause phase separation or microstructural instability after ball milling and SPS.
Industrial scalability of the proposed method remains uncertain.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis states that the method enables large-scale processing, while the uncertainty field says that scalability to industrial levels remains uncertain.

Cu is presented as posing a significant positive-heat-of-mixing problem in the hypothesis and baseline, but the material-initial-state field describes Cu or analogous additions as 'low-mixing enthalpy elements.'
